about: Content for Vulnerabilities.html (the 'Hidden weak spots' page under Learn). Text is written for young readers. Facts about each CVE come from CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue and the reports listed in 'sources'. Re-check with: python scripts/check_vulnerability_data.py

glossary.plain: A weak spot in an app: a mistake in its code that attackers could use.
glossary.like: A window that doesn't lock properly.

glossary.plain: The trick that uses the weak spot.
glossary.like: Someone climbing in through that window.

glossary.plain: An ID for one known weak spot, so everyone talks about the same one.
The fix, sent out by the company that made the app.
A weak spot attackers use before any fix exists.
glossary.like: A broken lock nobody knew about yet.

glossary.plain: A public list, kept by the US cyber agency CISA, of weak spots attackers are known to really use.

parts.means: The name of the list: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures.
The year this ID was given out.
Its own number, so no two weak spots share an ID.

examples.arrived: A Word document sent by email, or a link to one.
examples.trap: Opening the document, or even just previewing it, let the attacker run their own program on the computer. It didn't need macros.
examples.lesson: Be careful with documents you weren't expecting, even ones that look ordinary.

examples.arrived: Spam emails with document attachments, written in many languages.
examples.trap: Opening the attachment quietly downloaded a harmful program onto the computer.
examples.fixed: Fixed in 2017, yet attackers were still using it in 2019 against computers that had never updated.
examples.lesson: An old bug only works on you if you skip updates.

sources.title: Infosecurity Magazine: Microsoft warns of campaign exploiting 2017 bug

examples.arrived: An email or meeting invite with a booby-trapped reminder sound.
examples.trap: As soon as the email arrived, Outlook contacted the attacker's computer and leaked a scrambled copy of the user's login password.

click.text: Nothing. Arriving in the inbox was enough

examples.lesson: Updates protect you even from traps you would never see.

examples.nickname: The fake picture in a ZIP
examples.app: WinRAR, an app that opens ZIP and RAR files
examples.arrived: ZIP files posted on online trading forums, pretending to be trading tips.
examples.trap: Inside was what looked like a picture. Clicking it ran a hidden program instead, which was used to get into people's trading accounts.
examples.lesson: Apps you rarely open need updating too.

examples.arrived: An iMessage with a booby-trapped image attached, sent by the attacker.
examples.trap: The phone handled the image by itself, and the attacker could install spyware. It was aimed at a few chosen people, not at everyone.
examples.lesson: Install phone updates soon, even when you didn't do anything wrong.

examples.app: Chrome, Edge, Firefox and other apps that show WebP pictures
examples.arrived: A specially made web page with a broken picture on it.
examples.trap: Browsers show pictures automatically, and this one could let the attacker run code inside the browser.
examples.lesson: When your browser asks to restart, say yes: that's when the fix goes in.

quiz.question: What does a software update often contain?
options: Fixes for weak spots attackers could use
quiz.explain: Updates often close weak spots. Every example on this page was stopped by an update.

quiz.question: A stranger sends you a ZIP file you weren't expecting. What's the safest move?
options: Open it to see what's inside
Rename it first, then open it
Don't open it. Ask someone you trust, or delete it
quiz.explain: The WinRAR trap hid a program behind what looked like a picture. Unexpected files are best left closed.

quiz.question: In CVE-2023-23397, what does "2023" tell you?
options: The year the ID was given out
quiz.explain: A CVE ID is the list name, the year the ID was given out, and its own number.

quiz.question: Which habit protects you even from traps you can't see?
options: Keeping your apps and phone updated
quiz.explain: Two examples here needed no click at all. Only an update stopped them.
